explanations.explanation: Fire it is. The text says fire from the LORD blazed among them and consumed the outskirts of the camp. It hit the edges, not the middle, and I think that matters. Any baker knows what it's like when a smoke alarm goes off and the whole room gets quiet in one second.

Hail is a real thing the LORD sent in Egypt (Exodus 9:23), so I see why it came to mind. But here the text says fire from the LORD blazed among the people. It burned the outskirts of the camp, and no ice was involved. I've pulled enough hot trays to say fire and hail feel very different.

Darkness did come over Egypt for three days (Exodus 10:22), so it's a fair guess. Here, though, the text says fire from the LORD blazed among the people and consumed the outskirts of the camp. That's a bright problem, not a dark one. Trust me, friend, I've sat in real darkness in a drawer, and this was not that.

Moses it is. The text says the people cried out to Moses, and he prayed to the LORD, and the fire died down. They came to the one who was leading them, and he took it straight to the LORD. That's a good habit for any of us when things start burning.

Aaron was Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), so he's a natural guess. But the text here says the people cried out to Moses. Moses is the one who prayed, and then the fire died down. Aaron just isn't in this scene.

Joshua is Moses' attendant, and he does show up later in this passage. In this moment, though, the text says the people cried out to Moses. Moses prayed to the LORD, and the fire died down. Good name to know, just not the one on this card.

explanations.answer: The fire of the LORD burned there
explanations.explanation: That's it. The text says the place was called Taberah, "because the fire of the LORD had burned among them." The place carried a name that reminded everybody what happened there. I carved my name into a handle once, and honestly, a name sticks around a long time.

explanations.answer: Water flowed from a rock there
explanations.explanation: Water from a rock is a real story, but it's a different one (Exodus 17:6). Here the text gives its own reason for the name Taberah: the fire of the LORD had burned among them. So this place got named for the fire. The water story keeps its own spot.

explanations.answer: The people rested there for days
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about resting at Taberah. It gives one reason for the name, which is that the fire of the LORD had burned among them. Moses prayed, the fire died down, and the place got its name. When the text hands you the reason, friend, take it.

Meat. They say, “Who will feed us meat?” The craving came from the rabble among them, and then the Israelites picked it up too. They had food already, but they wanted something else. I know a thing or two about wanting what's across the kitchen.

Bread is close to something real, because the LORD rained down bread from heaven for them (Exodus 16:4). That's the manna they already had. What they cried out for here was meat. So it wasn't more bread they wanted, it was something else.

Honey is a sweet guess, and the manna did taste like wafers made with honey (Exodus 16:31). But that's what they already had. The people weeping here ask, “Who will feed us meat?” So the answer is meat, not honey.

Egypt. They remember the fish they ate freely there, along with the cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic. The word that jumps out at me is "freely." Their memory of that menu is doing a lot of work for them.

Midian is where Moses went when he fled Egypt (Exodus 2:15), so it's a real place with a real Moses connection. But the people here say they remember the fish they ate freely in Egypt. That's where all the food memories are coming from. Midian isn't on this menu.
Sinai is where they had just set out from (Numbers 10:12), so it's close by. But the people say they remember the fish they ate freely in Egypt. They're looking back, not at where they just were.

True. They say, “But now our appetite is gone; there is nothing to see but this manna!” That's their complaint in their own words. They look around the camp, see the same thing they always see, and the longing starts.
This one is true, friend. The people really do say, “But now our appetite is gone; there is nothing to see but this manna!” Their complaint is about the manna. That's what they were looking at.

That's the one. The text says the manna "tasted like pastry baked with fine oil." Everybody in that camp had a bakery's worth of flavor falling from the sky, and they were still complaining. I'd have hired a taster for that.

That one sounds like a tough lunch. But the text says the manna tasted like pastry baked with fine oil. Nothing about vinegar anywhere in these verses. The cakes were closer to something I'd pull out of my own oven.

The text doesn't say salt anywhere here. It says the manna tasted like pastry baked with fine oil. They ground it, crushed it, boiled it or shaped it into cakes. A good baker could do a lot with that.
True. The text says when the dew fell on the camp at night, the manna fell with it. So it showed up with the dew, right at the camp. Nobody had to preheat anything.
The text says this one is true. When the dew fell on the camp at night, the manna fell with it. It came down with the dew, and that's how the camp got it. Now I'm jealous all over again.

Displeased. The text says Moses heard the people weeping at the entrances to their tents, and “…Moses was also displeased.” It was a lot to hear, family after family. I bet he heard it in his sleep, too.

Patient is a kind guess, but it's not what the text says. It says the anger of the LORD was kindled greatly, and “…Moses was also displeased.” Moses was running low, and the rest of the chapter shows it.

The text doesn't say Moses was sympathetic here. It says “…Moses was also displeased.” He heard the weeping at the tents and it landed hard on him. I think he was tired, and the next verses sound like it.

That's right. Moses says the LORD told him, “Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries an infant.” Then he asks whether he conceived these people or gave them birth. That's a lot of baby for one man to hold.

A shepherd carrying a lamb is a real picture in Scripture (Isaiah 40:11). It's just not the one Moses uses here. He says he's told to carry them as a nurse carries an infant. So the picture on this card is the nurse.

The eagle picture shows up elsewhere, when God says He bore Israel on eagles' wings (Exodus 19:4). But Moses doesn't use it here. He says he's been told to carry them as a nurse carries an infant. Different moment, different picture.
Moses says the opposite. His words are, “I cannot carry all these people by myself; it is too burdensome for me.” So he's telling the LORD it's too much for one man. The answer on this card is False.

False is right. Moses says, “I cannot carry all these people by myself; it is too burdensome for me.” He tells the LORD plainly it's too much. Notice he brings it to the LORD instead of keeping it in.
That's what he says, and I think this part is heavy. Moses asks, “please kill me right now.” He's worn all the way down and says so to the LORD. I'm not going to joke about this one, friend.
Moses never asks to go back to Egypt. That's the people's idea, not his. What he asks is for the LORD to kill him right now. I think this is a heavy moment, and I'd rather sit with it than say more.
Aaron is Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), but he doesn't come up here at all. Moses asks the LORD to kill him right now. It's a heavy verse, and I think it shows how low he'd gotten.

explanations.answer: Help Moses bear the burden of the people
explanations.explanation: Yes. The LORD says, “They will help you bear the burden of the people, so that you do not have to bear it by yourself.” Moses had just said he couldn't carry them alone. And here's the LORD answering that very thing.

explanations.answer: Gather the manna for the whole camp
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give the elders that job. The people were already gathering the manna themselves (Numbers 11:8). The LORD says the elders will help Moses bear the burden of the people. That's the work He has for them.

explanations.answer: Carry the ark ahead of the people
explanations.explanation: The ark did go ahead of them (Numbers 10:33), but that's not what this passage gives the elders. The LORD says they will help Moses bear the burden of the people. So their job here is helping Moses, not carrying the ark.
Month. The LORD says they'll eat it “but for a whole month.” He counts the days up first: one or two, then five or ten or twenty. Then He says month. That's a long stretch with one menu.
A year is a long time, friend, but the text doesn't go that far. The LORD counts one or two days, then five or ten or twenty, and lands on a whole month. That's the length He names.
Season is close in spirit, but it's not the word. The LORD counts through one or two days, then five or ten or twenty, then says a whole month. A month is the number He gives.

explanations.answer: They rejected the LORD who is among them
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives. The LORD says, “…because you have rejected the LORD, who is among you…” They also cried out, “Why did we ever leave Egypt?” It's about turning away from the LORD, not just about food.

explanations.answer: They gathered too much of the manna
explanations.explanation: The text never says that. The LORD's reason is, “…because you have rejected the LORD, who is among you…” Manna isn't the problem He points to. The problem is how they treated Him.

explanations.answer: They left the mountain of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's not the reason the LORD gives. What they cried out was, “Why did we ever leave Egypt?” and He says it's because they rejected the LORD, who is among them. So it's about Egypt and about Him, not about leaving a mountain.

True. Moses asks, “If all our flocks and herds were slaughtered for them, would they have enough? Or if all the fish in the sea were caught for them, would they have enough?” He's doing the math out loud. And it doesn't add up for him.

The text says this is true. Moses asks whether slaughtering all the flocks and herds would be enough. Then he asks about all the fish in the sea. He's counting the numbers and not seeing how it works.
They prophesy. The text says the LORD took some of the Spirit on Moses and placed it on the seventy elders. “As the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied…” That's the sign the Spirit was on them.
No altar here. The text says the LORD placed some of the Spirit on the seventy elders. “As the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied…” That's what they do.
Quiet would be a fair guess, but they weren't silent. The text says, “As the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied…” So the answer is that they prophesy.
The text says the opposite. The elders did prophesy when the Spirit rested on them, but the text says they never did so again. So it happened that once. The answer on this card is False.
False is right. The Spirit rested on the seventy elders and they prophesied, and the text says they never did so again. It was a one-time moment. I know a thing about moments that only come once.

explanations.answer: The Spirit rests on them and they prophesy
explanations.explanation: That's what happens. Eldad and Medad were listed but hadn't gone out to the tent, “…and the Spirit rested on them.” They prophesied right there in the camp. That's a surprise for two guys who stayed home.

explanations.answer: They are sent away from the camp for good
explanations.explanation: Nobody sends them anywhere. The text says they had stayed in the camp, and the Spirit rested on them. They prophesied in the camp. Staying put turned out to be the right spot for them.

explanations.answer: They are struck down for staying behind
explanations.explanation: Nothing like that happens to them. The text says they were among those listed but hadn't gone out to the tent. “…and the Spirit rested on them,” and they prophesied in the camp. It's good news for them.
That's what Joshua says. He's Moses' attendant, and he speaks up: “Moses, my lord, stop them!” Eldad and Medad were prophesying in the camp. Joshua wanted it shut down.
Blessing would've been a kind response, but it's not what Joshua says. His words are, “Moses, my lord, stop them!” He wants Moses to put a stop to it. Moses answers him next.
Joshua doesn't ask for that. He says, “Moses, my lord, stop them!” Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp, and he wants it stopped. Bringing them to the tent isn't in the text.

Prophets. Moses says, “I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets and that the LORD would place His Spirit on them!” He isn't bothered by Eldad and Medad. He's glad about it, and he wants more of it.
Elders is a fair guess because of the seventy. But Moses says, “I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets…” He's talking about all the LORD's people, not a smaller group. Prophets is the word.

Priests doesn't come up in his answer. Moses says, “I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets and that the LORD would place His Spirit on them!” That's the wish he voices to Joshua. He wants the Spirit on everybody.

explanations.answer: A day's journey in every direction
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. The quail are brought near the camp “for a day’s journey in every direction around the camp.” That's a lot of ground to cover in birds. I'd hate to be the one holding the broom.

explanations.answer: A stone's throw on just one side
explanations.explanation: That's far too small. The text says the quail came for a day's journey in every direction around the camp. Not one side, and not a short throw. It surrounded the whole camp.

explanations.answer: Only the ground around the tent
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't narrow it down to the tent. It says the quail came about two cubits above the ground, for a day's journey in every direction around the camp. That covers the whole camp, not one spot.
The text says otherwise. “All that day and night, and all the next day, the people stayed up gathering the quail.” That's well past one morning. They stayed up gathering it, so the answer is False.

False is right. “All that day and night, and all the next day, the people stayed up gathering the quail.” They kept at it through the night and into the next day. Nobody was headed back to the tents early.
That's what the text says. “…the LORD struck them with a severe plague.” It happened while the meat was still between their teeth. This part is heavy, friend.
Hail did fall in Egypt (Exodus 9:23), but it isn't what happens here. The text says the LORD struck the people with a severe plague. This is a heavy verse, so I'll keep it simple.

A flood is a real thing in Scripture, back in Noah's day (Genesis 7:17), but it isn't what happens here. The text says the LORD struck the people with a severe plague. This is one of the heavy parts of the chapter.

Craved. The text says they called the place Kibroth-hattaavah, “…because there they buried the people who had craved other food.” This is a sad name, and I think it's meant to be remembered. The place carries that story.
Refused is close in feeling, but it's not the word. The text says, “…because there they buried the people who had craved other food.” The name remembers the craving. It's a heavy name.

Nothing is said about stealing here. The text says they called the place Kibroth-hattaavah, “…because there they buried the people who had craved other food.” The word is craved. I think it's one of the weightier lines in the chapter.
